Main.sentence: Europe is a ___E:continent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continent)___ [t] located entirely in the ___E:Northern Hemisphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Hemisphere)___ and mostly in the ___E:Eastern Hemisphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Hemisphere)___ .

It is bordered by the ___E:Arctic Ocean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Ocean)___ to the north, the ___E:Atlantic Ocean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean)___ to the west, the ___E:Mediterranean Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea)___ to the south, and ___E:Asia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia)___ to the east. Europe shares the ___E:landmass U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landmass)___ of ___E:Eurasia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasia)___ with Asia, and of ___E:Afro-Eurasia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Eurasia)___ with both ___E:Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa)___ and Asia.   Europe is commonly considered to be ___E:separated from Asia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boundaries_between_the_continents#Asia_and_Europe)___ by the ___E:watershed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_divide)___ of the ___E:Ural Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ural_Mountains)___ , the ___E:Ural River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ural_(river))___ , the ___E:Caspian Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea)___ , the ___E:Greater Caucasus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Caucasus)___ , the ___E:Black Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea)___ , and the ___E:Turkish straits U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_straits)___ .

Europe covers approx. 10,186,000 square kilometres (3,933,000 sq mi), or 2% of ___E:Earth's surface U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth#Surface)___ (6.8% of Earth's land area), making it the second-smallest continent (using the ___E:seven-continent model U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continent#Number)___ ). ___E:Politically U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Europe)___ , Europe is divided into about ___E:fifty sovereign states U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sovereign_states_and_dependent_territories_in_Europe#UN_member_states_and_UNGA_non-member_observer_state)___ , of which ___E:Russia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia)___ is the ___E:largest U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_European_countries_by_area)___ and ___E:most populous U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_European_countries_by_population)___ , spanning 39% of the continent and comprising 15% of ___E:its population U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Europe)___ .

Europe had a total population of about 745 million (about 10% of the ___E:world population U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population)___ ) in 2021; the ___E:third-largest U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_continents_and_continental_subregions_by_population)___ after Asia and Africa.

The ___E:European climate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_of_Europe)___ is affected by warm Atlantic currents, such as the ___E:Gulf Stream U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream)___ , which produce a ___E:temperate climate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperate_climate)___ , tempering winters and summers, on much of the continent.
Further from the sea, seasonal differences are more noticeable producing more ___E:continental climates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_climate)___ .

The ___E:culture of Europe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_Europe)___ consists of a range of national and regional cultures, which form the central roots of the wider ___E:Western civilisation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_culture)___ , and together commonly reference ___E:ancient Greece U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece)___ and ___E:ancient Rome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome)___ , particularly through ___E:their Christian successors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity_in_Europe)___ , as crucial and shared roots.

Beginning with the ___E:fall of the Western Roman Empire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire)___ in 476 CE, ___E:Christian consolidation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianization)___ of Europe in the wake of the ___E:Migration Period U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migration_Period)___ marked the European ___E:post-classical U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-classical)___ ___E:Middle Ages U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages)___ .

The ___E:Italian Renaissance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Renaissance)___ spread across many ___E:Western European U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Europe)___ countries, adapting to local contexts and giving rise to distinct national expressions.

The renewed ___E:humanist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_humanism)___ emphasis on ___E:art U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_art)___ and ___E:science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_in_the_Renaissance)___ was among the several factors that contributed to the broader transition to the modern era. Since the ___E:Age of Discovery U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Discovery)___ , led by ___E:Spain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire)___ and ___E:Portugal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire)___ , Europe played a predominant role in global affairs with multiple explorations and conquests around the world.

Between the 16th and 20th centuries, ___E:European powers colonised U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_former_European_colonies)___ at various times the ___E:Americas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas)___ , almost all of Africa and ___E:Oceania U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceania)___ , and the majority of Asia.

The ___E:Age of Enlightenment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment)___ , the ___E:French Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution)___ , and the ___E:Napoleonic Wars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars)___ shaped the continent culturally, politically, and economically from the end of the 17th century until the first half of the 19th century.

The ___E:Industrial Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution)___ , which began in ___E:Great Britain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain)___ at the end of the 18th century, gave rise to radical economic, cultural, and social change in ___E:Western Europe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Europe)___ and eventually the wider world.

Both ___E:world wars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_war)___ began and were fought to a great extent in Europe, contributing to a decline in Western European dominance in world affairs by the mid-20th century as the ___E:Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union)___ and the United States took prominence and competed over ___E:ideological dominance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideological_dominance)___ and ___E:international influence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_influence)___ in Europe and globally.

The resulting ___E:Cold War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War)___ divided Europe along the ___E:Iron Curtain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Curtain)___ , with ___E:NATO U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO)___ in the ___E:West U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Bloc)___ and the ___E:Warsaw Pact U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Pact)___ in the ___E:East U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Bloc)___ .

This divide ended with the ___E:Revolutions of 1989 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_of_1989)___ , the ___E:fall of the Berlin Wall U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Berlin_Wall)___ , and the ___E:dissolution of the Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Soviet_Union)___ , which allowed ___E:European integration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_integration)___ to advance significantly.

European integration has been advanced institutionally since 1948 with the founding of the ___E:Council of Europe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Europe)___ , and significantly through the realisation of the ___E:European Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union)___ (EU), which represents today the majority of Europe.

The European Union is a ___E:supranational U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supranational_union)___ political entity that lies between a ___E:confederation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederation)___ and a ___E:federation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation)___ and is based on a system of ___E:European treaties U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_treaties)___ .

The EU originated in Western Europe but has been ___E:expanding eastward U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlargement_of_the_European_Union)___ since the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. A majority of its members have adopted a common currency, the ___E:euro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro)___ , and participate in the ___E:European single market U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_single_market)___ and ___E:a customs union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union_Customs_Union)___ .

A large bloc of countries, the ___E:Schengen Area U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schengen_Area)___ , have also abolished internal border and immigration controls. ___E:Regular popular elections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_to_the_European_Parliament)___ take place every five years within the EU; they are considered the second-largest democratic elections in the world after ___E:India's U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_India)___ .
The ___E:EU economy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_the_European_Union)___ is the second-largest in the world by nominal GDP and third-largest by PPP-adjusted GDP.

In classical ___E:Greek mythology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_mythology)___ , ___E:Europa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(consort_of_Zeus))___ ( ___E:Ancient Greek U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language)___ : Εὐρώπη , Eurṓpē ) was a ___E:Phoenician U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenicia)___ princess.

One view is that her name derives from the Ancient Greek elements εὐρύς ( eurús ) 'wide, broad', and ὤψ ( ōps , ___E:gen. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genitive_case)___ ὠπός , ōpós ) 'eye, face, countenance', hence their composite Eurṓpē would mean 'wide-gazing' or 'broad of aspect'.

Broad has been an ___E:epithet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epithet)___ of Earth herself in the reconstructed ___E:Proto-Indo-European religion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Indo-European_mythology)___ and the poetry devoted to it.  An alternative view is that of ___E:Robert Beekes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_S._P._Beekes)___ , who has argued in favour of a pre-Indo-European origin for the name, explaining that a derivation from eurus would yield a different ___E:toponym U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toponymy)___ than Europa.

Beekes has located toponyms related to that of Europa in the territory of ancient Greece, and localities such as that of ___E:Europos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europus_(Almopia))___ in ___E:ancient Macedonia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonia_(ancient_kingdom))___ .

There have been attempts to connect Eurṓpē to a Semitic term for west , this being either ___E:Akkadian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akkadian_language)___ erebu meaning 'to go down, set' (said of the sun) or ___E:Phoenician U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenician_language)___ 'ereb 'evening, west',  which is at the origin of ___E:Arabic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic)___ maghreb and ___E:Hebrew U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_language)___ ma'arav . ___E:Martin Litchfield West U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Litchfield_West)___ stated that "phonologically, the match between Europa's name and any form of the Semitic word is very poor",  while Beekes considers a connection to Semitic languages improbable.
Most major world languages use words derived from Eurṓpē or Europa to refer to the continent.

Chinese, for example, uses the word Ōuzhōu ( 歐洲 / 欧洲 ), which is an abbreviation of the transliterated name Ōuluóbā zhōu ( 歐羅巴洲 ) ( zhōu means "continent"); a similar Chinese-derived term Ōshū (欧州) is also sometimes used in Japanese such as in the Japanese name of the European Union, Ōshū Rengō (欧州連合) , despite the ___E:katakana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katakana)___ Yōroppa (ヨーロッパ) being more commonly used. In some Turkic languages, the originally Persian name Frangistan ("land of the ___E:Franks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franks)___ ") is used casually in referring to much of Europe, besides official names such as Avrupa or Evropa .

The prevalent definition of Europe as a geographical term has been in use since the mid-19th century.

Europe is taken to be bounded by large bodies of water to the north, west and south; Europe's limits to the east and north-east are usually taken to be the ___E:Ural Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ural_Mountains)___ , the ___E:Ural River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ural_(river))___ , and the ___E:Caspian Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea)___ ; to the south-east, the ___E:Caucasus Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caucasus_Mountains)___ , the ___E:Black Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea)___ , and the waterways connecting the Black Sea to the ___E:Mediterranean Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea)___ .

Islands are generally grouped with the nearest continental landmass, hence ___E:Iceland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland)___ is considered to be part of Europe, while the nearby island of Greenland is usually assigned to ___E:North America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America)___ , although politically belonging to Denmark.
Nevertheless, there are some exceptions based on sociopolitical and cultural differences.

Cyprus is closest to ___E:Anatolia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatolia)___ (or Asia Minor), but is considered part of Europe politically  and it is a member state of the EU. Malta was considered an island of ___E:North-western Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maghreb)___ for centuries, but now it is considered to be part of Europe as well.  "Europe", as used specifically in ___E:British English U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_English)___ , may also refer to ___E:Continental Europe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Europe)___ exclusively.

The term "continent" usually implies the ___E:physical geography U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_geography)___ of a large land mass completely or almost completely surrounded by water at its borders.

Prior to the adoption of the current convention that includes mountain divides, the border between Europe and Asia had been redefined several times since its first conception in ___E:classical antiquity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_antiquity)___ , but always as a series of rivers, seas and straits that were believed to extend an unknown distance east and north from the Mediterranean Sea without the inclusion of any mountain ranges.

Cartographer ___E:Herman Moll U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Moll)___ suggested in 1715 Europe was bounded by a series of partly joined waterways directed towards the Turkish straits, and the ___E:Irtysh River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irtysh_River)___ draining into the upper part of the ___E:Ob River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ob_River)___ and the ___E:Arctic Ocean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Ocean)___ .

In contrast, the present eastern boundary of Europe partially adheres to the Ural and Caucasus Mountains, which is somewhat arbitrary and inconsistent compared to any clear-cut definition of the term "continent".

The current division of Eurasia into two continents now reflects ___E:East-West U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East%E2%80%93West_dichotomy)___ cultural, linguistic and ethnic differences which vary on a spectrum rather than with a sharp dividing line. The geographic border between Europe and Asia does not follow any state boundaries and now only follows a few bodies of water.

Turkey is generally considered a ___E:transcontinental country U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_transcontinental_countries)___ divided entirely by water, while Russia and ___E:Kazakhstan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakhstan)___ are only partly divided by waterways.

France, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain are also transcontinental (or more properly, intercontinental, when oceans or large seas are involved) in that their main land areas are in Europe while pockets of their territories are located on other ___E:continents U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continents)___ separated from Europe by large bodies of water.

Spain, for example, has territories south of the ___E:Mediterranean Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea)___ —namely, ___E:Ceuta U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceuta)___ and ___E:Melilla U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melilla)___ —which are parts of ___E:Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa)___ and share a border with Morocco.
According to the current convention, Georgia and Azerbaijan are transcontinental countries where waterways have been completely replaced by mountains as the divide between continents.

The first recorded usage of Eurṓpē as a geographic term is in the ___E:Homeric Hymn U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeric_Hymn)___ to ___E:Delian Apollo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delian_Apollo)___ , in reference to the western shore of the ___E:Aegean Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aegean_Sea)___ .

As a name for a part of the known world, it is first used in the 6th century BCE by ___E:Anaximander U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anaximander)___ and ___E:Hecataeus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecataeus_of_Miletus)___ .

Anaximander placed the boundary between Asia and Europe along the Phasis River (the modern ___E:Rioni River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rioni_River)___ on the territory of ___E:Georgia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(country))___ ) in the Caucasus, a convention still followed by ___E:Herodotus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herodotus)___ in the 5th century BCE.  Herodotus mentioned that the world had been divided by unknown persons into three parts—Europe, Asia, and Libya (Africa)—with the ___E:Nile U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile)___ and the Phasis forming their boundaries—though he also states that some considered the ___E:River Don U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_River_(Russia))___ , rather than the Phasis, as the boundary between Europe and Asia.  Europe's eastern frontier was defined in the 1st century by geographer ___E:Strabo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strabo)___ at the River Don.  The Book of Jubilees described the continents as the lands given by ___E:Noah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noah)___ to his three sons; Europe was defined as stretching from the ___E:Pillars of Hercules U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillars_of_Hercules)___ at the ___E:Strait of Gibraltar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strait_of_Gibraltar)___ , separating it from ___E:Northwest Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Africa)___ , to the Don, separating it from Asia.

The convention received by the ___E:Middle Ages U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages)___ and surviving into modern usage is that of the ___E:Roman era U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_era)___ used by Roman-era authors such as ___E:Posidonius U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posidonius)___ ,  ___E:Strabo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strabo)___ ,  and ___E:Ptolemy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemy)___ ,  who took the Tanais (the modern Don River) as the boundary.
The Roman Empire did not attach a strong identity to the concept of continental divisions.

However, following the fall of the ___E:Western Roman Empire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire)___ , the ___E:culture that developed in its place U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_culture)___ , linked to Latin and the Catholic church, began to associate itself with the concept of "Europe".
The term "Europe" is first used for a cultural sphere in the ___E:Carolingian Renaissance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolingian_Renaissance)___ of the 9th century.

From that time, the term designated the sphere of influence of the ___E:Western Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Church)___ , as opposed to both the ___E:Eastern Orthodox U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox)___ churches and to the ___E:Islamic world U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_world)___ .

A cultural definition of Europe as the lands of ___E:Latin Christendom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christendom)___ coalesced in the 8th century, signifying the new cultural condominium created through the confluence of Germanic traditions and Christian-Latin culture, defined partly in contrast with ___E:Byzantium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantium)___ and ___E:Islam U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam)___ , and limited to northern ___E:Iberia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberia)___ , the British Isles, France, Christianised western Germany, the Alpine regions and northern and central Italy.

The concept is one of the lasting legacies of the ___E:Carolingian Renaissance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolingian_Renaissance)___ : Europa often [dubious – discuss] figures in the letters of Charlemagne's court scholar, ___E:Alcuin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcuin)___ .

The transition of Europe to being a cultural term as well as a geographic one led to the borders of Europe being affected by cultural considerations in the East, especially relating to areas under Byzantine, Ottoman, and Russian influence.
Such questions were affected by the positive connotations associated with the term Europe by its users.
Such cultural considerations were not applied to the Americas, despite their conquest and settlement by European states.
Instead, the concept of "Western civilisation" emerged as a way of grouping together Europe and these colonies.

The question of defining a precise eastern boundary of Europe arises in the Early Modern period, as the eastern extension of ___E:Muscovy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsardom_of_Russia)___ began to include ___E:North Asia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Asia)___ .

Throughout the Middle Ages and into the 18th century, the traditional division of the landmass of ___E:Eurasia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasia)___ into two continents, Europe and Asia, followed Ptolemy, with the boundary following the ___E:Turkish Straits U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_Straits)___ , the ___E:Black Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea)___ , the ___E:Kerch Strait U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerch_Strait)___ , the ___E:Sea of Azov U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_of_Azov)___ and the ___E:Don U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_River_(Russia))___ (ancient ___E:Tanais U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanais)___ ).

But maps produced during the 16th to 18th centuries tended to differ in how to continue the boundary beyond the Don bend at ___E:Kalach-na-Donu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalach-na-Donu)___ (where it is closest to the Volga, now joined with it by the ___E:Volga–Don Canal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volga%E2%80%93Don_Canal)___ ), into territory not described in any detail by the ancient geographers.

Around 1715, ___E:Herman Moll U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Moll)___ produced a map showing the northern part of the ___E:Ob River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ob_River)___ and the ___E:Irtysh River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irtysh_River)___ , a major tributary of the Ob, as components of a series of partly joined waterways taking the boundary between Europe and Asia from the Turkish Straits, and the Don River all the way to the Arctic Ocean.

In 1721, he produced a more up to date map that was easier to read. However, his proposal to adhere to major rivers as the line of demarcation was never taken up by other geographers who were beginning to move away from the idea of water boundaries as the only legitimate divides between Europe and Asia.
Four years later, in 1725, ___E:Philip Johan von Strahlenberg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Johan_von_Strahlenberg)___ was the first to depart from the classical Don boundary.

He drew a new line along the ___E:Volga U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volga_River)___ , following the Volga north until the ___E:Samara Bend U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samara_Bend)___ , along ___E:Obshchy Syrt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obshchy_Syrt)___ (the ___E:drainage divide U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_divide)___ between the Volga and ___E:Ural Rivers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ural_River)___ ), then north and east along the latter waterway to its source in the ___E:Ural Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ural_Mountains)___ .
At this point he proposed that mountain ranges could be included as boundaries between continents as alternatives to nearby waterways.
Accordingly, he drew the new boundary north along ___E:Ural Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ural_Mountains)___ rather than the nearby and parallel running Ob and Irtysh rivers.
This was endorsed by the Russian Empire and introduced the convention that would eventually become commonly accepted.

However, this did not come without criticism. ___E:Voltaire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voltaire)___ , writing in 1760 about ___E:Peter the Great U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_the_Great)___ 's efforts to make Russia more European, ignored the whole boundary question with his claim that neither Russia, Scandinavia, northern Germany, nor Poland were fully part of Europe.

Since then, many modern analytical geographers like ___E:Halford Mackinder U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halford_Mackinder)___ have declared that they see little validity in the Ural Mountains as a boundary between continents.
The mapmakers continued to differ on the boundary between the lower Don and Samara well into the 19th century.

The ___E:1745 atlas U:(https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Atlas_of_Russian_Empire._1745_year)___ published by the ___E:Russian Academy of Sciences U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Academy_of_Sciences)___ has the boundary follow the Don beyond Kalach as far as ___E:Serafimovich U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serafimovich_(town))___ before cutting north towards ___E:Arkhangelsk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkhangelsk)___ , while other 18th- to 19th-century mapmakers such as ___E:John Cary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cary)___ followed Strahlenberg's prescription.

To the south, the ___E:Kuma–Manych Depression U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuma%E2%80%93Manych_Depression)___ was identified c. 1773 by a German naturalist, ___E:Peter Simon Pallas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Simon_Pallas)___ , as a valley that once connected the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea,   and subsequently was proposed as a natural boundary between continents.

By the mid-19th century, there were three main conventions, one following the Don, the ___E:Volga–Don Canal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volga%E2%80%93Don_Canal)___ and the Volga, the other following the Kuma–Manych Depression to the Caspian and then the Ural River, and the third abandoning the Don altogether, following the ___E:Greater Caucasus watershed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Caucasus_watershed)___ to the Caspian.
